g.text: Cold-to-warm. Entertain or inspire, then start selling. (17 new formats)
N21 AI Story VSL (Cinematic Caption Story)
g.textArea:
What it is: A 45-120s story-VSL told entirely through AI-generated, film-look scenes with burned-in captions (often with VO): it opens on a humiliating or emotional moment from the buyer's or spouse's point of view ('At 43 I had to ask for an XXL', 'My wife came home and froze'), shows the struggle and failed fixes, reveals the hidden cause with a 3D mechanism shot, then the product, the transformation scenes and a guarantee/offer close. No real presenter carries the ad.

Why it works: Gets the emotional pull of a long advertorial story with cinematic visuals you could never afford to shoot; best for problem-aware supplements and health/wellness products with a 'hidden cause' angle.

How to make one: 1) Write a 60-90s first-person (or spouse's) story script: embarrassing moment -> 'I was doing everything right' -> real hidden cause -> product -> life after -> guarantee. 2) Generate one consistent AI character across 10-15 cinematic scenes plus 1-2 3D mechanism shots (organ/cell glow), and burn each script line on as a caption. 3) Close on real product-in-hand footage and the offer (guarantee, bundle, 'link below').

Closest format already on the board: Personal Story [TOF,MOF] - same story arc, but here no creator is on camera: the whole story is acted out in AI cinematic scenes with captions/VO, plus a built-in mechanism reveal like a VSL.

g.text: N22 BTS vs Final Shot Reveal
g.textArea:
What it is: Opens on the raw behind-the-scenes setup (rig, tripod, suction mount, studio) capturing a shot, then cuts to the polished final footage it produced, alternating setup vs result a few times and ending on the brand card.

Why it works: Proves the product's output quality directly - the viewer sees exactly what they'd get - ideal for tools that produce a result (camera gear, lighting, editing, beauty tools).

How to make one: 1) Film the product set up doing its job in a plain/messy real environment (the 'how'). 2) Capture or render the clean final result it produces (the 'wow'). 3) Cut setup > result 2-4 times with a 'POV: no crew, just this' caption, end on product + offer.

Closest format already on the board: Product Demo Ads - a demo shows use; this hinges on the contrast reveal between the scrappy setup and the polished output it created.

What it is: The whole ad is one transformation: opens on the 'before' (shaggy hair in the barber chair, frizzy curls, a 'Day 0' body/face), the middle shows the product doing the work (a pro cutting and styling with it, or an AI morph sliding from Day 0 to Day 90), and it closes on the big 'after' reveal plus product card/offer.

Why it works: A visible change from bad to great is the strongest proof there is and the viewer watches to see the reveal; use for hair, skin, body, cleaning or any product with a visual result. Live-action (salon/barber chair) builds trust, the AI-morph version is a cheap 10s test.

How to make one: 1) Pick the most dramatic 'before' you can show (real client in the chair, or an AI-generated Day 0 image) with a hook caption like 'every transformation…' or 'Face fat? gone'. 2) Show the product in action mid-ad: pro applying/styling it, or a smooth morph with the product pack sitting in frame. 3) Hold on the 'after' (turn, hair flip, Day 90 label), then cut to a clean product shot with price/offer.

Closest format already on the board: Challenge / Case Studies - those follow a person over days or break down a result in talk; here the ad is just the before → product → after reveal, either a live makeover or an AI morph.

What it is: A real famous person fronts the ad as the brand's spokesperson: opens on the celebrity's face/name delivering the hook to camera (selfie-style or studio), intercuts product close-ups and demo b-roll with kinetic claim supers while they keep talking, and closes back on them with a sign-off + logo/shop card.

Why it works: The face stops the scroll and transfers trust/status instantly; works when a recognizable person (even a niche micro-celebrity or known pro) can credibly endorse the product.

How to make one: 1) Book the most recognizable face your niche respects (micro-celebrity, known athlete/chef/creator) and have them open with their name or a personal hook. 2) Intercut their lines with 4-6 hero product/demo shots, each with one bold claim super. 3) Close on them saying a one-line endorsement, then logo + offer card.

Closest format already on the board: Celebrity Podcast Clip (Borrowed Authority): that borrows a real podcast clip; here the celebrity is hired and speaks directly as the brand's paid presenter.

What it is: A polished, agency-grade commercial with no one talking to camera: it opens on a striking cinematic shot (location, model or CGI product), cuts through a music-led montage of styled lifestyle, macro texture or CGI product shots (often one short feature super per shot), and closes on a logo/wordmark or offer end card.

Why it works: Sells a premium mood and perceived brand size instead of an argument, so it lifts trust and price tolerance for aesthetic or giftable products, especially to warm-ish audiences and as a retargeting/brand layer.

How to make one: 1) Pick one setting/mood that matches the buyer's aspiration (rainy city, golden-hour beach, moody studio) or render the product in CGI. 2) Shoot 8-12 slow, well-lit shots: product hero, macro textures, hands/model using it; add one 2-4 word benefit super per shot, no voiceover. 3) Cut to a licensed music track and end on a clean logo + offer card.

Closest format already on the board: Satisfying B-roll (Front-Splice) / Product Demo Ads: those buy attention or show function; this is a whole wordless TV-style brand spot selling mood and premium perception.

What it is: A music-only, campaign-quality model shoot of the product: opens on a wide hero shot of the model in a styled location or studio, cuts between turns, back views and macro fabric/detail close-ups (often several looks or colourways), and closes on a logo or offer end card. No talking, no story, no claims.

Why it works: For fashion, swim and jewellery the garment is the pitch: a polished shoot makes the piece look premium and aspirational in 6-20s, and it scales cheaply into one ad per SKU or drop.

How to make one: 1) Book one model and one strong location or seamless backdrop; shoot each piece wide, walking, turning, back view and 3-4 macro detail shots. 2) Cut fast to a trending or moody track (1 shot per ~1s), alternating full-body hero with fabric/detail close-ups; optionally add 'Introducing X' / 'New in' super. 3) End on a clean logo/offer card (e.g. '10% off everything', 'Shop the edit').

Closest format already on the board: Try-On Haul - a haul is a creator trying on pieces on her phone and reacting; this is a brand's polished, silent editorial shoot of the product with no creator persona.

What it is: Native phone-shot clip of one person in ONE complete outfit: opens mid-pose (mirror selfie, bedroom, doorway, street), then she turns, walks, twirls and shows front/back/detail to music, with a single relatable one-line caption ('dinner and drinks fit', 'never taking these off', 'what I'm wearing as a size 12'). No talking, no demo, no multiple outfits.

Why it works: It looks exactly like an organic TikTok/IG OOTD post, so it slips past ad blindness and shows true fit and movement on a real body; perfect for one hero garment.

How to make one: 1) Put one creator in the full outfit (hero product + simple styling) in a real home/street spot; film handheld or propped phone, 8-15s. 2) Capture walk-in, slow turn, back view, hand-on-fabric detail and a confident end pose, cut to a trending sound. 3) Add one native-style caption line (POV / occasion / size), no logo until the end or watermark only.

Closest format already on the board: Try-On Haul - a haul shows several pieces back to back; a fit check commits the whole ad to one outfit with no talking.

What it is: Creator opens undone (robe, casual clothes, bare face) with a 'get ready / get dressed with me' hook, chats or captions through each step as she applies or puts on the product (makeup, skincare, outfit), and ends on the finished look reveal, often with a walk-out or twirl.

Why it works: The before-to-done arc is a built-in curiosity loop that holds viewers to the reveal, and the chatty native format lets the product be used naturally instead of pitched.

How to make one: 1) Start the creator 'before' (robe, messy hair, no makeup) on camera with a 'GRWM for ___' text hook tied to an occasion. 2) Film each step of using the product in order with casual chat or captions (what it is, why she likes it); keep cuts quick. 3) End on the full reveal: final look, turn or walk-out, plus product/offer card.

Closest format already on the board: UGC How-To - a how-to teaches usage step by step; GRWM is a native lifestyle ritual with chat, built around a transformation reveal and an occasion.

What it is: A hype launch for a limited-edition product co-branded with a franchise or another brand: opens on the two logos locked up ('X x Y', 'Limited Edition'), shows the co-branded pack in the franchise's world with VFX/action beats and a quick product-in-use moment, and closes on a 'limited time only / before it's gone' scarcity card.

Why it works: Borrows a fandom's existing excitement and adds scarcity, so it pulls both fans and existing buyers into an urgent purchase; use for drops, seasonal editions and collabs.

How to make one: 1) Create a limited edition (collab with a creator/brand/local artist, or a seasonal theme) and design a co-branded pack. 2) Open on the 'X x Y Limited Edition' lockup, then 3-5 dramatic VFX/themed shots of the pack plus one quick use shot. 3) Close on 'Limited time only - gone when it's gone' with the shop link.

Closest format already on the board: Reaction / Trend-Hijack (Borrowed Fame): that disguises borrowed attention as native content; this is an official co-branded product launch trailer with a scarcity close.

What it is: A cinematic 30s documentary vignette of one real, named person (athlete, mom, founder) with a name/title lower-third: they narrate their own life and routine in VO over observational footage, the product appears as part of that routine, and it closes on logo + tagline.

Why it works: Feels like documentary truth rather than a testimonial pitch, so the claim rides on a real identity the viewer aspires to; great for supplements, fitness and performance products.

How to make one: 1) Find one real customer with an aspirational identity (triathlete, busy mom, fighter) and record a 2-min audio interview about their routine. 2) Shoot observational b-roll of their day (training, kitchen, family) with the product used naturally; add a name/title lower-third early. 3) Cut the best 5-6 VO lines over the footage with small captions, end on logo + tagline.

Closest format already on the board: UGC Testimonial / Personal Story: those are selfie talk-to-camera; this is a produced observational doc with VO and a named lower-third.

What it is: A relatable person states a problem and the confusion ('hundreds of products... which one do I even need?'), says an expert built a short quiz, then a screen recording walks through the quiz questions and the 'calculating your results' screen, closing on 'take the free 2-minute quiz, link below'.

Why it works: Sells a free personalised answer instead of a product, lowering friction for cold traffic and segmenting buyers into the right SKU.

How to make one: 1) Build a 4-6 question quiz that routes to your product/bundle (Typeform, Octane AI, Shopify quiz app). 2) Film a person with the problem + 'which one do I need?' confusion, then screen-record answering the quiz. 3) End on the results-loading screen and a 'take the free quiz' CTA.

Closest format already on the board: Q&A - there the creator answers a question; here the call-to-action is the quiz itself and the ad demos taking it.

g.text: N32 Torture Test (Try To Break It)
g.textArea:
What it is: The whole ad is a sequence of escalating abuse or stress attempts on the product (flips, jumps, drops, water, weight) with it surviving each one, ending on the verdict shot ('still in / still works') and brand.

Why it works: Visual proof of durability or fit beats any claim and the escalation keeps people watching to see if it finally fails.

How to make one: 1) List 5-7 increasingly extreme tests relevant to your product's promise (falls out? breaks? leaks?). 2) Film each in one clean shot with a short caption, hardest test last. 3) End on the intact product + a 'still going' verdict and offer.

Closest format already on the board: Product Demo Ads / Challenge - a demo shows normal use; this is a pure escalating stress test where survival is the payoff.

What it is: The whole ad is paced by an on-screen clock or progress bar: it opens on the promise/first use, then each beat jumps forward in time (8:03pm > 8:14pm, or 5 sec > 15 min > 5 days > 2 weeks) with one caption saying what the product is doing at that moment, and closes on the end-state result + offer.

Why it works: Turns a vague benefit into a concrete, believable sequence of milestones and makes viewers stay to see the final timestamp.

How to make one: 1) List 4-6 real milestones of using the product (first seconds, first session, day 5, week 2) with one benefit each. 2) Film or animate one shot per milestone with a big timestamp/progress bar overlay that advances every beat. 3) End on the final milestone result, then cut to product + offer card.

Closest format already on the board: Challenge ('I tried X for 7 days') - this is not a creator challenge diary; the timer/progress bar itself is the structure and can run in minutes inside one session or as an animated graphic.

g.text: N34 This or That (Pick Your Vibe)
g.textArea:
What it is: Two product variants shown side by side under a fixed header ('Choose your spooky season vibe', 'Same but different'), each labelled by name, swapping to a new pair every 1-2s for 6-8 rounds so the viewer silently picks, then ending on a full collection grid + shop CTA.

Why it works: Turns browsing into a game: every pair is a micro-decision that keeps the viewer watching, shows the whole range fast, and makes them mentally pick a favourite before the CTA; ideal for products with many SKUs.

How to make one: 1) Pick 12-16 variants (colours, shapes, scents) and pair them; film each pair side by side in the same framing (e.g. two fingers, two hands, two items). 2) Add a fixed 'Choose your ___ vibe' header and name labels; cut a new pair every ~1.5s. 3) Close on a grid of the whole collection with 'Shop the collection' / offer badge, and ask 'which one are you?' in copy.

Closest format already on the board: Ranking / Tier List - a tier list ranks options with your product on top; this lets the viewer pick between your own variants with no ranking or competitor.

What it is: Rapid paired montage for a custom/made-to-order product: opens on a caption like 'the stones our clients chose vs the rings we made', then alternates 'the stone' / 'the inspiration' shots with the finished piece made from it, and closes on 'design yours' with the brand logo.

Why it works: Each pair is a mini reveal that proves craftsmanship and makes the viewer imagine their own version; ideal for personalised/custom products (custom jewellery, pet portraits, photo gifts, engraved items).

How to make one: 1) Collect 4-8 pairs of customer input (photo, stone, sketch, inspiration image) and the finished product made from it. 2) Cut them as quick labelled pairs ('the photo' / 'the portrait') over trending music, close-up and hand-held. 3) End on a line like 'Send us yours / design your own' with the logo and offer.

Closest format already on the board: Product Comparison Video - that compares against a competitor or old method; here each pair is the customer's raw input next to the custom piece made from it.

What it is: A first-person 'I looked into it' story told almost entirely through phone screens: opens on a call screen or Google search ('I called my water company' / 'does legal water mean safe'), moves through real-looking web pages, databases, stats and a review card as evidence, then reveals the product as the fix with a before/after number and closes on the offer.

Why it works: Screen evidence feels like the viewer's own research, so the problem reads as discovered fact rather than an ad claim; great for invisible-problem products.

How to make one: 1) Write the investigation as 5-7 'then I found...' beats tied to a hidden problem your product fixes. 2) Screen-record each step (call screen, Google search typing, a stat page, a lookup tool, a review) with one caption per beat. 3) Finish with the product shown solving it (number before > after) and an offer card.

Closest format already on the board: Breakdown / Explainer - this is not a talking-head explanation; the whole ad is phone screen recordings acting as personal investigation evidence.

g.text: N37 Photoshop Fix ('Fixed It For You')
g.textArea:
What it is: Open on a real-looking 'problem' photo (plain room, old item), cut to a Photoshop screen recording where the item is erased and the product dropped in, then the edit comes alive as real footage of the product in that spot under 'Fixed it for you'.

Why it works: Borrows the 'fixed it for you' meme so the product reads as the obvious upgrade; very easy to copy for home, decor and lifestyle goods.

How to make one: 1) Shoot a still of the space/situation with the 'wrong' item. 2) Screen-record a quick Photoshop swap putting your product in. 3) Cut to real footage of the product in that exact spot being used, caption 'Fixed it for you'.

Closest format already on the board: Product Comparison Video - old vs new, but told through a meme photo-edit reveal instead of side-by-side.
